newsitem.title: UK: BBC gives assurances over World Service changes.
newsitem.headline: BBC gives assurances over World Service changes.

text.p: The British Broadcasting Corporation agreed on Monday to safeguards sought by the government to ensure that sweeping management changes do not damage the quality of the BBC's prized World Service.

Ministers and members of parliament reacted with alarm in June when BBC Director-General John Birt announced plans to save money by integrating the World Service more closely with the public service broadcaster's domestic news-gathering operations.
They voiced fears for the distinctive nature of the World Service, which broadcasts in more than 40 languages and has an estimated 140 million regular listeners.

Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, whose ministry funds the World Service to the tune of 178 million pounds ($280 million) a year, set up a working group with the BBC to examine the implications of the restructuring.
The working party recommended 20 measures that were accepted by Rifkind and Birt on Monday at a 30-minute meeting.
The steps aim "to ensure the continued protection of World Service interests and the maintenance of the special character, style, ethos and quality" of its broadcasts.
With the safeguards in place, Rifkind and Birt said in a statement that the restructuring could bring substantial benefits for the World Service.

In a retreat from its original plans, the BBC agreed that World Service news programmes should continue to be made by a separate staff and that journalists preparing English broadcasts should continue to work alongside foreign-language staff.
Other safeguards give World Service programme commissioners full editorial responsibility and the right to cover particular events or to respond to breaking news.
Critics of Birt's original blueprint had been concerned that the BBC would give domestic coverage priority over sending correspondents to foreign troublespots.

Although some World Service staffers said they remained sceptical, a Foreign Office spokesman described the changes as substantial and said they should give genuine reassurance to the BBC's critics. "It's a victory for the World Service," he said.
